title: The Heat Kernel and the Cauchy Problem

items.title: The heat operator, the heat equation, and the Cauchy problem
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open in the space-time variable $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$. The heat operator is $\partial_t-\Delta_x$, where $\Delta_x$ is the Laplacian in the $n$ spatial coordinates; a classical solution of the heat equation on $\Omega$ is a $u\in C^2(\Omega)$ with $\partial_tu-\Delta_xu=0$ on $\Omega$, and the inhomogeneous equation is $\partial_tu-\Delta_xu=f$ for a prescribed source $f$. A Cauchy problem for the equation on a space-time domain consists of the equation together with initial data $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$ prescribed on the time-zero slice; values prescribed on the lateral (spatial) boundary of the domain are boundary data. Initial and spatial boundary data are different sets of constraints and are not interchanged.
items.strategy: Specialise the published scalar-PDE vocabulary to the linear second-order operator $\partial_t-\Delta_x$ on an open space-time domain: the time variable is the last coordinate, the spatial Laplacian is the published one of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], and classical solutions are $C^2$. Its principal symbol is positive definite, so the published parabolic classification applies and separates this equation from the Laplace and wave equations. Initial data live on the $t=0$ slice, lateral boundary data on the spatial boundary. The definition itself uses no choice axiom.

items.title: The heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$ and its causal extension
items.statement: For $n\ge1$ and $t>0$ the heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$ is the function $$\Gamma(x,t):=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4t}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,$$ where $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ is the Euclidean square. It is positive and $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$. Its causal extension is $\Gamma(x,t)$ for $t>0$ and $\Gamma(x,t):=0$ for $t\le0$; the displayed formula is not evaluated at $t=0$ as a function value. The normalisation is fixed by the unit-mass identity of the next lemma, and the causal extension is used only as a locally integrable function or, after embedding, as a distribution.
items.strategy: Unpack the formula: the Gaussian is a composite of the published real exponential with the quadratic form of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], so it is $C^\infty$ on the open set $t>0$ by the published closure of $C^k$ Euclidean maps under algebra and composition; positivity is immediate from the exponential. The $t\le0$ clause is a definition, not a pointwise limit, and its distributional reading is discharged in [[thm-heat-kernel-is-the-causal-fundamental-solution]]. No choice axiom is needed for the definition.

items.title: Normalisation, parabolic scaling, heat equation and derivative bounds for the heat kernel
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling: $\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there, $\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$ there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with $|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and $(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.
items.strategy: Unit mass: substitute $x=(4t)^{1/2}u$, factor the $n$-dimensional Gaussian into one-dimensional factors by Tonelli/Fubini and integrate with the published one-dimensional Gaussian integral; the same substitution gives (ii), which pins the $\lambda$-dependence. Part (iii) is a coordinate computation with the published chain/product closure of $C^k$ Euclidean maps and Clairaut–Schwarz for the mixed second derivatives. Part (iv) follows from (ii) in the form $D^\alpha\Gamma(x,t)=t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}(D^\alpha\Gamma)(x/\sqrt t,1)$, the polynomial-times-Gaussian decay of the fixed profile $\Gamma(\cdot,1)$, and the elementary inequality that a Gaussian beats any polynomial. The approximate-identity clauses are (i), the unit $L^1$-bound, and the tail clause $\int_{|x|>\delta}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$, read off from (ii). This carries the Countable Choice cost of the change-of-variables and product-measure theorems.

items.title: First and second Gaussian heat-kernel moments
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$ and $t>0$, all first and second moments are absolutely integrable and $\int x_i\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=0$, $\int x_ix_j\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=2t\delta_{ij}$. In particular $\int |x|^2\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=2nt$.
items.strategy: Factor the product Gaussian with Tonelli. Absolute integrability follows from polynomial times Gaussian decay. Oddness gives the first and off-diagonal moments. For the diagonal integrate $x^2e^{-x^2/(4t)}=-2tx(d/dx)e^{-x^2/(4t)}$ over $[-R,R]$ by parts, and let $R\to\infty$; the boundary term vanishes and the integral is $2t$ times the Gaussian mass. The remaining coordinates each have mass1.

items.title: Gaussian kernels form an approximate identity
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$, the kernels $\Gamma_t$ are positive with unit mass and $\|\Gamma_t\|_1=1$. For every $\delta>0$, $\int_{|x|>\delta}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$. Thus they form an $L^1$ approximate identity.
items.strategy: The original normalisation lemma supplies positivity and unit mass. Set $x=\sqrt t z$; the tail is $\int_{|z|>\delta/\sqrt t}\Gamma(z,1)\,dz$, which tends to0 by dominated convergence. These are exactly the published definition clauses; this separates a previously folded claim without deleting that clause from its original supplier.

items.title: The heat kernel semigroup identity $\Gamma_t*\Gamma_s=\Gamma_{t+s}$
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For all $s,t>0$ the convolution $\Gamma(\cdot,t)*\Gamma(\cdot,s)$ converges absolutely at every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and equals $\Gamma(x,t+s)$; that is, $\Gamma_t*\Gamma_s=\Gamma_{t+s}$ as functions on $\mathbb R^n$.
items.strategy: Write the convolution integrand as a product of Gaussians and complete the square in the integration variable $y$: the exponent becomes a perfect square in $y$ plus the cross term $-|x|^2/(4(t+s))$. The remaining Gaussian integral is evaluated with the published one-dimensional Gaussian integral and Tonelli/Fubini for the absolutely convergent integral. The prefactor $(4\pi t)^{-n/2}(4\pi s)^{-n/2}(4\pi ts/(t+s))^{n/2}$ equals $(4\pi(t+s))^{-n/2}$, which is the stated identity.

items.title: The causal heat kernel is the fundamental solution of the heat operator
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let $\Gamma$ be the causal extension of the heat kernel. Then $\Gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^{n+1})$, and its regular distribution $u_\Gamma\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^{n+1})$ satisfies $(\partial_t-\Delta)u_\Gamma=\delta_{(0,0)}$, that is, $$\langle(\partial_t-\Delta)u_\Gamma,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0,0)\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{n+1}),$$ so the causal extension is a fundamental solution of $\partial_t-\Delta$. Moreover $\Gamma(\cdot,t)\to\delta_0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ as $t\downarrow0^+$, that is, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\varphi(x)\,dx\to\varphi(0)$ for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$. The derivative $\partial_t$ is the distributional derivative in the last space-time coordinate.
items.strategy: Local integrability follows from unit mass and Tonelli on compact time slabs. For a compactly supported test $\varphi$, first work at $t\ge\varepsilon>0$ and integrate by parts in time and twice in each spatial coordinate by scalar integration by parts and Fubini; compact support removes the spatial boundary terms, including for n=1. The identity $\partial_t\Gamma=\Delta\Gamma$ cancels the two interior terms on this truncated region, giving $-\int_\varepsilon^\infty\int\Gamma(\partial_t\varphi+\Delta\varphi)=\int\Gamma(x,\varepsilon)\varphi(x,\varepsilon)dx$. Only after cancellation let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The omitted slab on the LEFT has absolute value at most $\varepsilon(\|\partial_t\varphi\|_\infty+\|\Delta\varphi\|_\infty)$ by unit mass. On the RIGHT replace $\varphi(x,\varepsilon)$ by $\varphi(x,0)$ with error at most $\varepsilon\|\partial_t\varphi\|_\infty$, and apply the approximate identity at0 to get $\varphi(0,0)$. Do not take separate dominated-convergence limits of $\int\partial_t\Gamma\varphi$ or $\int\Delta\Gamma\varphi$ near0: the crude $L^1$ bounds are of order1/t and not integrable. The weak Dirac limit is the same approximate-identity argument with a spatial test.

items.title: The heat evolution $H_t$ of initial data
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, and let $\Gamma$ be
the heat kernel of [[def-heat-kernel]], with $\Gamma_t:=\Gamma(\cdot,t)$ the
$L^1$ function of unit norm supplied by
[[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]]. Convolution is that
of [[def-convolution-of-two-functions-on-rn]], and $L^p$ means the class space
of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]].

For $t>0$ and $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ define $H_tf$ to be the $L^p$ class of
the function

$$x\longmapsto\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy.$$

By Young's convolution inequality [[thm-young-convolution-inequality]] applied
with the exponent triple $(p,1,p)$, which satisfies $1/p=1/p+1/1-1$, this
convolution is defined for almost every $x$ and belongs to $L^p$ with
$\|H_tf\|_p\le\|\Gamma_t\|_1\|f\|_p=\|f\|_p$; hence $H_tf$ is a well-defined
element of $L^p$ satisfying the contraction bound. For $p=\infty$ the integral
converges absolutely for every $x$ because
$|\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)|\le\|f\|_\infty\Gamma(x-y,t)$ almost everywhere in $y$, with
$\int\Gamma(x-y,t)\,dy=1$, so it defines a bounded representative with
$\|H_tf\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$.

The value depends only on the class of $f$: if $f=f'$ almost everywhere then the
null set where they differ is carried by translation to a null set
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]),
so at every $x$ the two $y$-integrands agree almost everywhere. Their absolute
convergence holds at the same points, and wherever they converge the integrals
agree by [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]. Each
$H_t$ is complex-linear on $L^p$, by linearity of the integral of each
representative.

Set $H_0f:=f$, the identity operator on $L^p$; the singular kernel formula is
never evaluated at $t=0$.
items.strategy: Young (p,1,p) gives the Lp class and contraction. For infinity the essential bound holds almost everywhere in the integration variable, and unit mass gives absolute convergence at every x. Equal representatives give equal integrable y-integrands wherever they converge. Define H0 as identity.

items.title: Spatial and time derivatives pass through heat convolution for positive time
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ (bounded measurable data are included). The absolutely convergent representative $u(x,t)=\int\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$ is $C^\infty$ for $t>0$, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ and $k\ge0$, $D_x^\alpha\partial_t^ku=(D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma_t)*f$. Moreover $|D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha,k}t^{-(n+|\alpha|+2k)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$. Domination is uniform on compact subsets $x\in K$, $\tau\le t\le T$ with $0<\tau<T<\infty$; $u_t=\Delta u$.
items.strategy: Use the smooth heat equation to write time derivatives as powers of the spatial Laplacian. Kernel Gaussian bounds put all derivatives in the conjugate Lp space, including the bounded endpoint. On compact positive-time intervals tau<=t<=T and bounded x, a single Gaussian majorant times |f| is integrable. Differentiate on open parameter intervals and use dominated convergence for joint continuity.

items.title: The heat Cauchy problem for bounded uniformly continuous data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let $u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define $u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)u_0(y)\,dy$ for $t>0$ and $u(x,0):=u_0(x)$. Then $u$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$, satisfies $\partial_tu=\Delta_xu$ there, is bounded with $\|u(\cdot,t)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty$, and converges locally uniformly at the initial time: $\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$ for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.
items.strategy: Bound the convolution by unit mass. Apply the earlier positive-time derivative-passing lemma at p=infinity for smoothness and the heat equation. The bounded continuous approximate-identity corollary supplies local uniform initial recovery.

items.title: The heat Cauchy problem for $L^p$ data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. For every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ the heat evolution of [[def-heat-evolution-of-initial-data]] satisfies: (i) $\|H_tf-f\|_p\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$; (ii) $\|H_tf\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ for every $t>0$; (iii) the semigroup law $H_{t+s}=H_tH_s$ on $L^p$ for all $s,t\ge0$, with $H_0$ the identity.
items.strategy: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity by [[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]], so the published $L^p$ approximate-identity theorem gives strong convergence. (ii) is Young's inequality for the pair $(p,1,p)$. (iii) Tonelli/Fubini applied to $|f|$ gives $\Gamma_t*(\Gamma_s*f)=(\Gamma_t*\Gamma_s)*f$ almost everywhere, the triple integral being finite because $\Gamma_t*\Gamma_s=\Gamma_{t+s}\in L^1$ by [[lem-heat-kernel-semigroup-identity]] and Young bounds the result in $L^p$; then $\Gamma_{t+s}*f=H_{t+s}f$. The case $t=0$ or $s=0$ is the operator identity $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ from the definition.

items.title: Uniqueness of strongly continuous mild heat solutions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$, $T>0$, $u\in C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb R^n))$, $u(0)=f$, and $u(t)=H_{t-s}u(s)$ for every $0<s<t\le T$. Then $u(t)=H_tf$ for all $0\le t\le T$. Hence the heat evolution is the unique solution in this class. This is uniqueness for the semigroup relation, not an unrestricted classical uniqueness assertion or a claim of strong continuity on all $L^\infty$.
items.strategy: Fix $t>0$ and $0<s<t$. By contraction and the semigroup law, $\|u(t)-H_tf\|_p=\|H_{t-s}(u(s)-H_sf)\|_p\le\|u(s)-f\|_p+\|f-H_sf\|_p$. Both terms tend to0 as $s\downarrow0$, by the given continuity and the published finite-p approximate identity result. Existence in $C([0,T];L^p)$ follows from continuity at0 and the semigroup law: right increments bounded by $\|H_hf-f\|_p$, left increments by the same quantity after applying $H_{t-h}$.

items.title: Heat generator at zero on compactly supported smooth data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$, $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ and $1\le p<\infty$, $\|(H_t\varphi-\varphi)/t-\Delta\varphi\|_p\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$.
items.strategy: Twice integrate by parts in each spatial coordinate to obtain d_s H_s phi=H_s Delta phi. Newton–Leibniz on [epsilon,t] and local uniform endpoint recovery of phi and Delta phi give the pointwise integral identity from zero. Joint positive-time smoothness supplies measurability; Minkowski and finite-p strong convergence show the averaged remainder tends to zero.

items.title: Mass conservation and positivity of the heat flow
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$, and let $H_t$ be the heat evolution. (i) If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ then $\int_{\mathbb R^n}H_tf(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\,dx$ for every $t>0$. (ii) If $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, $1\le p\le\infty$, satisfies $f\ge0$ almost everywhere, then $H_tf\ge0$ almost everywhere for every $t>0$.
items.strategy: (i) Tonelli applied to the nonnegative integrand $|f(y)|\Gamma(x-y,t)$ gives the iterated integral $\int\!\int\Gamma(x-y,t)|f(y)|\,dy\,dx=\|f\|_1<\infty$; translation invariance of Lebesgue measure makes the inner integral $\int\Gamma(x-y,t)\,dx=\int\Gamma=1$ for every $y$, so Fubini computes $\int H_tf=\int f$. (ii) The pointwise convolution of nonnegative measure-theoretic objects is nonnegative wherever it is finite, and the $L^p$ class of a nonnegative representative is nonnegative almost everywhere; the standard normalisation $H_t$ is linear so this is compatible with the definition.

items.title: Monotonicity and $L^p$ contractivity of the heat flow
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $1\le p\le\infty$. If $f,g\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfy $f\le g$ almost everywhere, then $H_tf\le H_tg$ almost everywhere for every $t>0$; and $\|H_tf\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ for every $f\in L^p$ and every $t\ge0$.
items.strategy: Apply the positivity clause of [[cor-heat-flow-preserves-mass-and-positivity]] to $g-f\ge0$ and use that $H_t$ is an $L^p$ linear operator (the pointwise convolution integral is linear where the integrals converge): $H_tg-H_tf$ is the class of $H_t(g-f)\ge0$. The contraction is part (ii) of [[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-lp-data]] for $p<\infty$ and Young's inequality with the pair $(\infty,1)$ for $p=\infty$; at $t=0$ it is the identity. All inequalities are almost-everywhere statements, as required for $L^p$ classes.

items.title: $L^p$ to $L^q$ smoothing estimate for the heat flow
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $1\le p\le q\le\infty$, and let $Q\in[1,\infty]$ be determined by $\frac1Q=1+\frac1q-\frac1p$. Then for every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $t>0$, $$\|H_tf\|_q\le C_{n,p,q}\,t^{-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}\|f\|_p,\qquad C_{n,p,q}:=(4\pi)^{-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}Q^{-\frac{n}{2Q}},$$ with the endpoint $Q=\infty$ (which occurs exactly at $p=1$, $q=\infty$) read as $Q^{-n/(2Q)}\to1$; for $p=q$ the constant is $1$ and the estimate is the contraction clause.
items.strategy: Young's convolution inequality with exponents $(p,Q,q)$ gives $\|\Gamma_t*f\|_q\le\|\Gamma_t\|_Q\|f\|_p$, and the scaling identity of [[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]] gives $\|\Gamma_t\|_Q=t^{-n(1-1/Q)/2}\|\Gamma_1\|_Q$. Substituting $x=\sqrt{4}\,u$ (or, equivalently, $x=\sqrt{4t}\,u$ in $\Gamma_t$) and using the Gaussian integral evaluates $\|\Gamma_1\|_Q=(4\pi)^{-n(1-1/Q)/2}Q^{-n/(2Q)}$; since $1-1/Q=1/p-1/q$ this is exactly the stated constant. When $p=q$ we have $Q=1$, the constants collapse to $1$, and the estimate is Young with the pair $(p,1,p)$. The exponent range $1\le p\le q\le\infty$ is precisely the Young range for a single application; no interpolation is claimed.

items.title: Spatial derivative estimates for the heat flow
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le q\le\infty$, and let $Q$ and the constants be as in [[thm-lp-to-lq-heat-kernel-estimate]]. For every multi-index $\alpha$, every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $t>0$, the function $x\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^n$, with $D^\alpha H_tf=(D^\alpha\Gamma(\cdot,t))*f$ as an absolutely convergent integral, and $$\|D^\alpha H_tf\|_q\le C_{n,p,q,\alpha}\,t^{-\frac{|\alpha|}{2}-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}\|f\|_p,\qquad C_{n,p,q,\alpha}:=\|D^\alpha\Gamma(\cdot,1)\|_Q<\infty.$$
items.strategy: The scaling identity gives $D^\alpha\Gamma_t(x)=t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}(D^\alpha\Gamma)(x/\sqrt t,1)$, hence $\|D^\alpha\Gamma_t\|_Q=t^{-|\alpha|/2}t^{-n(1-1/Q)/2}\|D^\alpha\Gamma_1\|_Q$, and $\|D^\alpha\Gamma_1\|_Q<\infty$ because $D^\alpha\Gamma_1$ is a polynomial times a Gaussian. Smoothness and the formula $D^\alpha H_tf=(D^\alpha\Gamma_t)*f$ follow by differentiating under the integral sign: the domination needed is exactly the derivative bound of [[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]], uniformly on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$, and Hölder's inequality makes the integral finite at every $x$. Young's inequality with exponents $(p,Q,q)$ then gives the estimate with the stated constant. Joint smoothness and the pointwise differentiation justification use [[lem-spatial-and-time-derivatives-pass-through-heat-convolution-for-positive-time]] with compact x/time domination, before applying Young for the displayed norms.

items.title: Spatial analyticity of heat flow at positive time
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$, $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, and $t>0$. Then $H_tf$ is real analytic on $\mathbb R^n$ (for complex data the real and imaginary parts are real analytic). For every $r>0$ and multi-index $\alpha$, $\|D^\alpha H_tf\|_\infty\le\alpha!r^{-|\alpha|}M_{n,p,t,r}\|f\|_p$, where $M_{n,p,t,r}=\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\exp(r\sum_i|x_i|/(2t)+nr^2/(4t))\|_{p\prime}<\infty$, $1/p+1/p\prime=1$. The spatial Taylor series converges absolutely and equals $H_tf(x+h)$ for every real $h$, uniformly for $h$ in each compact box. In particular taking $r=\sqrt t$ gives a factorial Gaussian derivative bound $C_{n,p}\alpha!t^{-|\alpha|/2-n/(2p)}\|f\|_p$.
items.strategy: Expand the translated Gaussian exponential in canonically indexed coordinates i<n. Bound the sum of regrouped coefficient moduli by B_r, which is dominated by a fixed Gaussian times exp(3nr²/(4t)). Holder and Tonelli make the integrated coefficients summable on each closed box; DCT gives the representative expansion. The holomorphic power-series theorem identifies coefficients with derivatives. Arbitrary r gives entire real spatial Taylor expansions; r=sqrt(t) gives the factorial bound, with essential-supremum scaling at the conjugate infinity endpoint.

items.title: Infinite propagation speed for nonnegative heat data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfy $f\ge0$ almost everywhere and $f\ne0$. Then for every $t>0$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ the everywhere-defined integral $H_tf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$ is strictly positive. In particular, if $f$ is compactly supported, nonnegative and nonzero, then the support of the solution at time $t$ is all of $\mathbb R^n$ for every $t>0$.
items.strategy: Let $A=\{f>0\}$. If $A$ had measure zero then $\int f=0$, so $A$ has positive measure and $\int f>0$ by the published zero-integral theorem. Fix $t>0$ and $x$. The integrand $\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)$ is nonnegative and is strictly positive for every $y\in A$, because the Gaussian is everywhere positive; hence it is positive on a set of positive measure and its integral is strictly positive. The support statement follows because the pointwise value is positive at every point of space.

items.title: Diffusivity, rescaling, and the heat kernel compared with the Poisson kernels
items.statement: With diffusivity parameter $\kappa>0$, the equation $u_t-\kappa\Delta u=0$ is converted into the $\kappa=1$ equation of this page by $v(x,t):=u(x,\kappa t)$, and its kernel is $\Gamma_\kappa(x,t)=(4\pi\kappa t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4\kappa t)}$; the kernel $\Gamma$ of this page is the case $\kappa=1$. The ball Poisson kernel $P_{R,a}(x,y)=(R^2-|x-a|^2)/(R\omega_{n-1}|x-y|^n)$ of [[thm-poisson-kernel-for-a-ball-in-rn]] is a boundary-value kernel: its two slots are an interior point and a boundary point, it carries no time parameter, and its dependence on $x$ is not translation-invariant convolution, so it is not the heat kernel in other notation. A normal-time Poisson kernel on a half-space does generate a semigroup, but with generator $-\sqrt{-\Delta}$ rather than $\Delta$, so the two one-parameter families are distinct; likewise the wave representation of a later page averages data on spheres of radius $ct$ instead of convolving with a positive kernel. A source's diffusivity normalisation must be matched before its kernel formula is quoted.
items.strategy: The rescaling is the chain rule: $\partial_tv(x,t)=\kappa\,\partial_tu(x,\kappa t)$ and $\Delta_xv(x,t)=(\Delta u)(x,\kappa t)$, so $v_t=\Delta v$ is equivalent to $u_t=\kappa\Delta u$. The comparison with the ball Poisson kernel is a statement about the two already-published objects and their normalisations: the ball kernel is not a convolution kernel in the interior variable and its normal-time analogue has the square-root generator, so it cannot be identified with $\Gamma$. This is a recorded convention remark, not a proof, and it consumes no later-page material.

items.title: Gaussian data remain Gaussian under the heat flow
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $\sigma>0$, and let
$f(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ be the density of the
centred Gaussian law with covariance $\sigma^2I_n$. Then
$f\in L^1\cap L^\infty$ and for every $t>0$ the heat evolution is the centred
Gaussian density with covariance $(\sigma^2+2t)I_n$,
$$H_tf(x)=\bigl(2\pi(\sigma^2+2t)\bigr)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(2(\sigma^2+2t))},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.$$
items.strategy: Under Countable Choice, identify f=Gamma_(sigma²/2), invoke the positive-time kernel semigroup identity, and apply the kernel moments at t+sigma²/2. Unit mass and the bounded Gaussian maximum give L1 and L-infinity membership.

items.title: The heat flow of an interval indicator is a difference of Gaussian tails
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n=1$ and let $f=\mathbf 1_{(a,b)}$ for real $a<b$. Then
$f\in L^p(\mathbb R)$ for every $1\le p\le\infty$ and, for every $t>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R$,
$$H_tf(x)=\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{b-x}{\sqrt{2t}}\Bigr)-\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{a-x}{\sqrt{2t}}\Bigr),$$
where $\Phi(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{u}e^{-s^2/2}\,ds$ is the standard
normal distribution function. In particular $H_tf$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R$ and strictly positive at every point for every $t>0$, while $f$ is
discontinuous.
items.strategy: The indicator of an interval is bounded and measurable, hence in every $L^p$, and $H_tf$ is its heat evolution of [[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-lp-data]]. Substitute $y=x+\sqrt{2t}\,s$ in the convolution integral: $\Gamma(x-y,t)\,dy$ becomes $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-s^2/2}ds$ and the interval of integration becomes $((a-x)/\sqrt{2t},(b-x)/\sqrt{2t})$, which is the stated difference of Gaussian tails. $\Phi$ is $C^\infty$ with $\Phi'=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}>0$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus, and $0<\Phi(u)<1$ at every finite $u$; strict positivity everywhere is also the compactly supported case of the infinite-propagation corollary.

items.title: The heat kernel is the self-similar solution with conserved mass
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $u(x,t):=\Gamma(x,t)$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$. Then $u$ solves the heat equation and is
invariant under parabolic dilations with amplitude $\lambda^n$:
$$u(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}u(x,t),\quad\text{equivalently}\quad\lambda^nu(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=u(x,t),\qquad\lambda>0,$$
and its total mass is conserved: $\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x,t)\,dx=1$ for every
$t>0$.
items.strategy: Direct substitution in the kernel formula for the scaling identity; the exponent $\lambda^{-n}$ is exactly the one that keeps the total mass fixed, which is the content of the scaling clause of [[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]]. Mass conservation is the unit-mass clause of the same lemma, and solving the heat equation is its identity $\partial_t\Gamma=\Delta\Gamma$.

items.title: The heat flow need not converge in supremum norm
items.statement:
Assuming Countable Choice, the claim that the $p=\infty$ endpoint can be added to the $L^p$ convergence
theorem for the heat flow, that is: for every
$f\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap\bigcap_{1\le p<\infty}L^p(\mathbb R)$ one has
$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|H_tf(x)-f(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$. This fails even
for the simplest jump data, and locally uniform convergence on compact sets
containing the jump fails as well. The same witnesses also obstruct convergence
in the essential supremum norm: for $f=\mathbf1_{[0,\infty)}$ one has
$H_tf(0)=1/2$ and $\|H_tf-f\|_\infty\ge1/2$; for
$f_0=\mathbf1_{[0,1)}$, which belongs to every finite $L^p$ and to $L^\infty$,
one has $H_tf_0(0)<1/2$ and $\|H_tf_0-f_0\|_\infty>1/2$ for every $t>0$. Thus the continuity hypothesis cannot be discarded;
actual supremum convergence for bounded real data requires uniform continuity,
and essential supremum convergence requires a uniformly continuous representative.
items.strategy: Use the half-line indicator only as bounded data: evenness gives H_tf(0)=1/2; it is not in finite Lp. Use the bounded interval indicator for the intersection class, with H_tf_0(0)<1/2. Spatial smoothness gives continuity, extending each jump error to an interval of positive measure and proving the essential supremum bound. Finite-p convergence applies only to the interval datum. The derivative estimate for p=q=infinity and the mean value theorem make each H_tg uniformly continuous; uniform-limit preservation establishes the necessity qualification for actual sup convergence and a uniformly continuous representative for essential-sup convergence.

items.title: The heat equation has no finite propagation speed
items.statement: Let $n=1$ and let $f=\mathbf 1_{[-1,1]}$, a nonzero nonnegative compactly supported $L^1$ function. Then for every $t>0$ the heat flow $H_tf$ is strictly positive at every $x\in\mathbb R$, so $\operatorname{supp}(H_tf)=\mathbb R$ for every $t>0$ although $\operatorname{supp}f=[-1,1]$. Heat data therefore propagate with infinite speed, in contrast with the wave equation's finite speed of propagation.
items.strategy: The indicator is a nonzero nonnegative element of $L^1$, so the infinite-propagation corollary applies: every point of space receives a strictly positive contribution from the everywhere-positive Gaussian at every positive time, and the support of the solution is the whole line immediately. This is a counterexample to finite propagation, not a new positivity proof.

items.title: The Fourier transform of the heat kernel
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and use the library's
$2\pi$-normalised transform
$\mathcal Ff(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx$ of
[[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]. Then for every $t>0$ the heat kernel
$\Gamma_t$ of [[def-heat-kernel]] is the $L^1$ function with
$$\mathcal F\Gamma_t(\xi)=e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2},\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
In the unnormalised convention
$\mathcal Gf(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)e^{-ix\cdot\xi}\,dx$ the same
computation reads $\mathcal G\Gamma_t(\xi)=e^{-t|\xi|^2}$. The heat-flow multiplier
$e^{-t|\xi|^2}$ alone does not determine the forward normalization: Hunter
uses $(2\pi)^{-n}\mathcal G$, whose transform of $\Gamma_t$ is
$(2\pi)^{-n}e^{-t|\xi|^2}$.
items.strategy: Apply the library Gaussian transform with s=1/(4pi t); the prefactors cancel and the exponent becomes -4pi²t|xi|². The phase-only convention uses G Gamma_t(xi)=F Gamma_t(xi/(2pi)). Hunter uses (2pi)^(-n)G; a heat multiplier alone does not identify forward normalization.

items.title: Heat evolution of affine and quadratic polynomials
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$ and $t>0$, define the Gaussian moment integrals directly for these polynomial data. They converge absolutely and give $H_t1=1$, $H_ty_i=x_i$, $H_t(y_iy_j)=x_ix_j+2t\delta_{ij}$, and $H_t|y|^2=|x|^2+2nt$. These integrals extend the convolution formula for this example; nonconstant polynomial data are not asserted to be in $L^p$ or bounded.
items.strategy: Substitute $z=x-y$, expand the affine/quadratic expressions, and use unit mass, vanishing first moments and covariance $2tI$ from the A-page moment lemma. Absolute convergence follows from the same moment estimates; no duplication of the Gaussian moment proof.

items.title: The heat smoothing time exponent is forced by scaling
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$ and $1\le p\le q\le\infty$, an estimate $\|H_tf\|_q\le Ct^{-\beta}\|f\|_p$ valid for every $t>0$ and every $f\in L^p$ with a finite constant independent of $t,f$ requires $\beta=\frac n2(1/p-1/q)$. This asserts the necessary power, not the optimal Young constant.
items.strategy: Choose a nonzero nonnegative indicator of the unit ball $f$. For $\lambda>0$ put $f_\lambda(x)=f(\lambda x)$, so $\|f_\lambda\|_p=\lambda^{-n/p}\|f\|_p$ with1/infinity=0. Kernel scaling gives $H_{\lambda^{-2}}f_\lambda(x)=H_1f(\lambda x)$ and its q norm is $\lambda^{-n/q}\|H_1f\|_q$, a finite positive number times that factor. The proposed bound implies $0<\|H_1f\|_q/\|f\|_p\le C\lambda^{2\beta-n(1/p-1/q)}$. Sending $\lambda$ to0 or infinity forces the exponent to0.
